Structural identifiability and Lie symmetries

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-symmetries.Rmd
methods-symmetries.Rmd

symmetryDetection() finds the Lie symmetries of the prediction with the Python package symident; a gauge or symmetryReduction() removes them. Guide: Symmetries.

Structural identifiability

The model is

\[\dot x = f(x, u(t), \theta), \qquad x(t_0) = x_0(\theta), \qquad y = g(x, \theta), \tag{1}\]

with states \(x\), input \(u\), observables \(y\) and parameters \(\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) of any kind, and prediction \(y(t; \theta) = g(x(t), \theta)\). It is locally structurally identifiable at \(\theta\) if no nearby \(\tilde\theta \ne \theta\) has the same prediction. The property depends on the equations alone, as if every observable were measured exactly and continuously, and the answer is the same for every \(\theta\) outside a set of measure zero, for generic \(\theta\). A structural non-identifiability makes the likelihood exactly flat along a curve, seen as a flat profile [1].

Lie symmetries

A Lie symmetry is a one-parameter group \(\Phi_\varepsilon\) on \(\Theta\) with \(y(t; \Phi_\varepsilon(\theta)) = y(t; \theta)\) for all \(t\) and small \(\varepsilon\). The orbits are the integral curves of the generator

\[X = \sum_{i=1}^d \xi_i(\theta)\, \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_i}, \qquad \xi(\theta) = \frac{\partial \Phi_\varepsilon(\theta)}{\partial \varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0}. \tag{2}\]

An invariant, \(X(I) = 0\), is constant on every orbit, and the prediction depends on \(\theta\) only through invariants. With \(r\) generators that span all symmetries and are independent at generic \(\theta\), the observables determine \(d - r\) parameter combinations.

Scalings, \(\xi_i(\theta) = w_i \theta_i\) with integer weights, are the most common symmetries of reaction networks; on the log scale their orbits are straight lines. Two kinds occur in almost every signaling model:

  • Observable s * (A + B) + off: concentrations of the moiety times \(\lambda\); the scale s and the rate constant of every term of second order in the moiety, or of first order in it in the equation of another state, divided by \(\lambda\). The generator moves the total, the scales and these rate constants together.
  • Unobserved intermediate: level and production rate times \(\lambda\), the rate it drives divided by \(\lambda\).

General symmetries also occur, such as a Möbius transformation of an input amplitude in an NFκB model [2]; symident finds generators with rational components.

Detection

With \(z = (x, \theta, t)\), \(\dot\theta = 0\), \(\dot t = 1\), the model is the vector field \(F = f\, \partial_x + \partial_t\), started at \(z_0(\theta) = (x_0(\theta), \theta, t_0)\). The Lie derivatives of the observables,

\[L_F^0 g = g, \qquad L_F^{k+1} g = F\bigl(L_F^k g\bigr), \tag{3}\]

at \(z_0\) are the time derivatives of the prediction at \(t_0\), so an analytic prediction is

\[y(t; \theta) = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(t - t_0)^k}{k!}\, L_F^k g\bigl(z_0(\theta)\bigr). \tag{4}\]

Collected up to order \(N\) they form \(\Psi_N(\theta)\), with the observability-identifiability matrix

\[\mathrm{OIM}_N(\theta) = \frac{\partial \Psi_N(\theta)}{\partial \theta}. \tag{5}\]

\(\Psi_N\) is constant on every orbit, \(\Psi_N(\Phi_\varepsilon(\theta)) = \Psi_N(\theta)\), and the derivative at \(\varepsilon = 0\) is, by the chain rule and (2),

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\Psi_N\bigl(\Phi_\varepsilon(\theta)\bigr)\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \mathrm{OIM}_N(\theta)\, \xi(\theta) = 0. \tag{6}\]

At generic \(\theta\) and large enough \(N\) the kernel of \(\mathrm{OIM}_N\) consists exactly of the generators, \(d - \operatorname{rank} \mathrm{OIM}_N\) counts them, and full rank means identifiable.

For scalings, (6) reads \(\mathrm{OIM}_N(\theta)\, \mathrm{diag}(\theta)\, w = 0\) for every \(\theta\). With rational right-hand sides, observables and initial values it holds where every term of every equation keeps the weighted degree, with weights on the states as well: a linear system in the weights, whose integer solution lattice symident computes exactly. A scaling that holds only on an invariant set, such as a start at rest, fails this test. It is among the remaining kernel vectors, the general directions, with closed forms from interpolation (symident method).

symident computes (5) exactly over finite fields \(\mathbb{F}_p\) at a fixed base point and takes the largest rank over several primes and a random point. The rank modulo \(p\) at a point can only fall below the generic value; the checks make a lower one unlikely but do not exclude it. symident proves the order \(N\) sufficient where it can. A direction is "exact" where the closed form is proven over the rationals, "verified" or "checked" where it is checked modulo a large prime at random points, with or without an error bound, and "open" without closed form; by default (reconstruct = FALSE) a general direction is returned as the support.

Steady-state starts, inputs and conditions

setting effect
equilibrate = TRUE initial state a root of \(f(x, 0, \theta) = 0\), inputs at 0
reduceCQ = TRUE one species eliminated per conserved moiety; freedom reported on the totals
forcings input states, 0 at rest
conditions shared parameters; a direction is non-identifiable only if it is so in every condition

symident writes an observable \(a \log g + c\) through \(g\). A clock-time factor of \(g\) such as \(e^{-\tau t}\) is no function of the states of a model at rest, so it is left out of the observables passed to symmetryDetection(); this is valid where the parameters of that factor take no part in a symmetry.

Gauge and reduction

Along every orbit the data term and the profiles of the data term are flat; a prior such as constraintL2() is not invariant and tilts them. The Hessian is flat in the generator directions at the optimum, in the Gauss-Newton approximation and for scalings on the log scale. So symmetries are removed before the fit. A gauge fixes one coordinate per scaling; each orbit meets the fixed values in one point with the same prediction. With \(W\) the weights of the scalings on the fixed coordinates, one row per generator, the gauge removes every scaling if

\[\det W \ne 0 . \tag{7}\]

symmetryReduction() turns the generators into a parameter transformation: for scalings a section fixing one coordinate per direction, for general directions invariants as new parameters (reduction).

Reference: symmetryDetection(), symmetryReduction()

[2]
B. Merkt, J. Timmer, and D. Kaschek, “Higher-order Lie symmetries in identifiability and predictability analysis of dynamic models,” Physical Review E, vol. 92, no. 1, p. 012920, 2015, doi: 10.1103/PhysRevE.92.012920.
